newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-New and old world cultures clash at air show.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-New and old world cultures clash at air show.

text.p: An anthropologist spending time at a big air show would find excellent machines and high-tech razamatazz but also detect a cultural clash between the American and European corporate mind.

For U.S. corporations, the visit to the Paris air show must seem like an excursion to an Old World theme park where European executives spend time looking over each other's assets and balance sheets but doing nothing much else.
Two years ago the industry talk at the last Paris air show was a merger between U.S. firms Lockheed and Martin Marietta to create a Godzilla with $24 billion in annual sales.
This time round, it is the merger between other U.S. giants, Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas, which will create a King Kong with $48 billion in annual turnover.
By contrast, the hesitant steps towards consolidation in the European aerospace industry were key issues raised by U.S. executives here at briefings tied to the air show.

They wanted to know what the newly-elected Socialist-led French government will do with defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF and whether a planned merger between state-owned Aerospatiale and warplane maker Dassault Aviation would get the go-ahead.
A sell-off of Thomson-CSF and the Aerospatiale-Dassault merger are seen as vital to rationalising European industry.
For Lockheed Martin executives, privatisation is a necessity before any real consolidation, on the view that a private company can act more freely than a state-controlled one.
"It's a strategic question for this country," a senior Lockheed Martin official said earlier this week.
"Governments are concerned about employment and getting re-elected," he said. As long as the state had a stake, moves by management to close factories would be fought by officialdom.
"Speed is essential," he said. If painful moves like closures had to be taken, they had to be done fast. They would preserve other jobs and increase value for shareholders.
Lockheed wants to form "equity relationships" with European companies, but it was not ready to enter the capital of state-controlled firms because of potential state intervention.
"Equity relationships give you the synergies and allow you to smash those blocks together," said a Lockheed executive.
Lockheed's "win rate" for business proposals stands at more than 60 percent since the merger two years ago, compared to an industry average of over 20 percent, the executive said.

The Lockheed Martin merger brought together capabilities which allowed it to gain business which might have eluded the two companies acting separately. The merger has resulted in savings of $2.6 billion and market capitalisation has increased by $15 billion since they came together.
Lockheed Martin is hiring over 2,000 engineers this year.
A senior executive at U.S. defence and aerospace group Raytheon sang from the same corporate hymn sheet at a separate briefing linked to the air show.

"If nothing changes structurally, you haven't changed anything," he said. "Europeans need centres of excellence," he said, adding that closures were needed to cut duplication and only the best of the merged companies should be retained.
Raytheon is merging with the defence activities of Hughes and acquiring the military operations of Texas Instruments (TI) to create a defence electronics business with annual sales of $11.6 billion.

It expects to cut costs by around 15 percent, worth some $1.7 billion, through the merger and acquisition -- "that's a very do-able number". Some 70 percent of the savings will be passed to the government, with Raytheon getting the rest.
Raytheon is also looking to hire around 2,000 engineers.

But one senior executive at Aerospatiale says that for all their talk of private sector efficiency, U.S. firms benefit from ample Pentagon research funds and long production runs only thanks to large government procurement contracts.
"In Europe, sovereignty is a big problem," a French executive said. Governments want to control programmes and keep factories within their own borders.
And unemployment is major concern. France's jobless rate stands at a record 12.8 percent and Germany has more than four million unemployed.
By contrast, a dynamic U.S. labour market cushions layoffs.

The French electorate rejected the austerity measures of the previous conservative government and voted in the present Socialist-led administration, which took a hostile view of privatisation in its election campaign.
"We know one day it will all be privatised but we have to take it step by step", the French aerospace executive said.
